content.text:
The Keeper of Gannet Rock

Every evening at a quarter past six, Elias Varn climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the Gannet Rock lighthouse. He counted them out loud. He had done it for thirty-one years, and in all that time the number had never changed, but he still counted, because the counting was part of the job, like trimming the wick or wiping salt off the lens.

The lighthouse stood on a black spur of rock four miles off the coast. A supply boat came every second Thursday with flour, tinned fish, paraffin, and letters. For the first decade the letters came from his sister in Aberdeen. After she died they came from nobody, and the boatman, a quiet man named Callum, began bringing newspapers instead. Elias read them weeks late and found that this suited him. By the time he heard about a crisis, it was usually over.

He kept a logbook with weather, ships sighted, and repairs. Some entries were longer than they needed to be. On the fourteenth of March he wrote that a gannet had landed on the gallery rail and looked at him for eleven minutes before flying off toward Norway. He had no way of knowing it went to Norway. He wrote it anyway.

In the autumn of his thirty-second year, a letter arrived with a government seal. The light was to be automated. A crew would come in spring to install an electric lamp, a timer, and a radio beacon. His services, the letter said, with what seemed like real regret, would no longer be required.

Elias read it twice, folded it into quarters, and put it in the logbook between October and November. That night he climbed the stairs, counted all hundred and twelve, and lit the lamp as usual. The beam swept across the water, and somewhere out in the dark a trawler captain saw it, adjusted his heading, and thought nothing more about it. That was how it was supposed to work. If the light did its job, nobody remembered it.

Winter was hard that year. A storm in January tore a shutter off the lamp room and sent spray up the tower so high that Elias found seaweed on the gallery the next morning. He repaired the shutter with planks from the storeroom and a box of nails gone orange with rust. He wrote in the log: Shutter repaired. Light maintained throughout. He did not mention that he had stood in the lamp room for nine hours holding a tarpaulin over the broken frame so the flame would not go out.

The engineers came in April. There were three of them, young and cheerful, and they called him sir. They worked fast. By the end of the week a sealed electric lamp sat where the old burner had been, ticking quietly to itself. One of them showed Elias how it switched on automatically at dusk.

"It'll never miss a night," the engineer said.

"No," Elias agreed. "I don't suppose it will."

On his last evening he climbed the stairs one more time. He counted. A hundred and twelve. He stood in the lamp room and watched the new light come on without him at exactly the right moment, and he found, to his surprise, that he did not mind. The ships would be safe. That had always been the point.

Callum took him ashore the next morning. Elias carried one bag and the logbook. Before they rounded the headland he looked back once. A gannet was circling the tower, turning in slow wide loops. Then it straightened and flew off toward Norway, or wherever gannets really go.
